concepts.title: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions
concepts.description: Java's exception hierarchy splits into checked exceptions, which the compiler forces every caller to handle or declare, and unchecked exceptions, which it does not. The split is not about severity: it separates anticipated, recoverable conditions outside your code from bugs in the code itself.
learningObjectives: Describe Java's Throwable hierarchy and where Error, Exception, and RuntimeException each sit within it.
Explain the precise compile-time rule that distinguishes a checked exception from an unchecked one.
Use throws to declare a checked exception a method might propagate, and explain what happens if you don't.
Explain the design rationale for the checked/unchecked split: recoverable external conditions vs programming bugs.
Identify common checked exceptions (IOException) and unchecked exceptions (NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException) from the standard library.
Critique the anti-pattern of catching a checked exception only to silently swallow it.

sections.heading: The Throwable Hierarchy: Error, Exception, and RuntimeException
sections.body:
Everything that can be thrown and caught in Java is a subclass of `Throwable`. `Throwable` has two direct subclasses with different meanings. `Error` represents serious problems signaled by the JVM, such as `OutOfMemoryError` or `StackOverflowError`, that application code generally cannot recover from and is not expected to catch. `Exception` is the base for conditions that a program might reasonably want to catch and respond to.

Under `Exception` there is a further split: `RuntimeException` and everything that extends it are **unchecked**. Every other subclass of `Exception`, meaning one that does *not* extend `RuntimeException`, is **checked**. `Error` and its subclasses are unchecked too, even though they sit outside `Exception`.

```text
Throwable
├── Error                     (unchecked -- OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError)
└── Exception
    ├── IOException            (checked)
    ├── SQLException           (checked)
    └── RuntimeException       (unchecked)
        ├── NullPointerException
        ├── ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
        ├── IllegalArgumentException
        └── ArithmeticException
```

Learn this tree, because the compiler does not decide checked or unchecked from how dangerous an exception sounds. It decides from *where the class sits in the tree*: whether it descends from `RuntimeException` (or `Error`).

sections.heading: The Compile-Time Rule: What Actually Makes an Exception 'Checked'
Why the Split Exists: Recoverable Conditions vs Programming Bugs
sections.body:
The distinction separates two kinds of failure and puts compiler pressure on only one of them. **Checked exceptions** are for conditions outside your program's own logic that a well-written caller can anticipate and recover from: a file that doesn't exist, a network connection that times out, a database that is briefly unreachable. None of these is a bug in the code that hit them. They are facts about the environment at a moment in time, and making every caller acknowledge them pushes you to think about those failures at API boundaries instead of pretending they can't happen.

**Unchecked exceptions**, overwhelmingly subclasses of `RuntimeException`, typically signal a bug in the code itself: dereferencing a `null` you shouldn't have, indexing past the end of an array, dividing by a value that should have been validated. Making every method up a deep call stack declare `throws NullPointerException` would convey almost nothing, since nearly any method could throw one given bad enough input. Checked exceptions earn their cost only when the set of things that can go wrong is small, specific, and worth naming in a method's public contract.

That is also why libraries *throw* unchecked exceptions such as `IllegalArgumentException` or `IllegalStateException` for API misuse (an invalid argument, or a call in the wrong state). These are programmer errors on the caller's side, to be fixed in code, not conditions to recover from at run time. Checked exceptions also have a practical cost you will meet soon: the standard functional interfaces such as `Function` and `Supplier` declare no checked exceptions, so a lambda body cannot throw one without wrapping it.

examples.title: A Checked Exception Forces Acknowledgment at Compile Time
examples.explanation: `FileReader`'s constructor is declared to throw `FileNotFoundException`, a checked exception (a subclass of `IOException`, itself a subclass of `Exception` that does not extend `RuntimeException`). `openBroken` neither wraps the call in `try`/`catch` nor declares `throws`, so `javac` produces no bytecode for this class and the program can never run in this broken state, which is the point of a checked exception. `openFixed` declares `throws IOException`, which accurately says that opening a file can fail for reasons outside the method's control, and leaves the decision on how to respond to whoever calls it.

examples.title: Unchecked Exceptions Compile Fine Without Any Declaration
examples.explanation: `divide` compiles without a single complaint, even though dividing by zero is a reachable failure mode: `ArithmeticException` extends `RuntimeException`, so it's unchecked, and the compiler never requires it to be caught or declared. Running this program prints "about to divide", then crashes with an uncaught `ArithmeticException: / by zero` before the second `println` ever executes. The JVM prints a stack trace to standard error and the process exits with a nonzero status. Nothing about this method's signature warned a caller that this could happen; that's a consequence of the checked/unchecked split, not an oversight: requiring every arithmetic method in existence to declare `throws ArithmeticException` would add ceremony to essentially every numeric method in the language for a condition that's fundamentally about a bad *value*, not an external, unpredictable condition.

misconceptions.description: Checked exceptions are for 'serious' failures, and unchecked exceptions are for 'minor' ones -- the split is basically about severity.
misconceptions.clarification: Severity has nothing to do with it. The split is: a checked exception is any subclass of `Exception` that does NOT also extend `RuntimeException`; everything else (`RuntimeException` and its subclasses, plus `Error` and its subclasses) is unchecked. `Error` covers some of the most severe conditions in the hierarchy (`OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`), and it is unchecked. The intended axis is whether the condition is external to the code and recoverable by a caller (checked), or typically a bug, or too pervasive to name in every signature (unchecked).

misconceptions.description: Wrapping a checked exception in a try/catch with an empty or purely log-and-continue catch block is a safe, harmless way to satisfy the compiler when you don't want to deal with it right now.
misconceptions.clarification: An empty or log-only catch block for a checked exception silences the compiler while throwing away the entire reason the exception existed: the program continues executing as if the operation had succeeded, even though it didn't. This is especially dangerous for checked exceptions, because the compiler's insistence on handling them was a signal that this failure mode is and worth thinking about. Swallowing it defeats that signal completely and tends to produce bugs that surface much later, far from the code that failed, and with no trace of the original cause left behind.
misconceptions.fact: An empty or log-only catch block for a checked exception silences the compiler while throwing away the entire reason the exception existed: the program continues executing as if the operation had succeeded, even though it didn't.

exercises.prompt: This code fails to compile with: `error: unreported exception FileNotFoundException; must be caught or declared to be thrown` (and a similar error for `readLine()`). Find the cause and fix it by propagating the checked exception correctly.
hints: Both `new FileReader(path)` and `reader.readLine()` are declared to throw checked exceptions. Neither is caught, and readFirstLine declares no throws clause.
You have two legitimate options: add a try/catch inside readFirstLine, or declare `throws IOException` on readFirstLine and let the caller (main) deal with it.

If you propagate with throws instead of catching, remember that main will then also need to either catch it or declare its own throws IOException, since the exception keeps propagating up the call chain.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `new FileReader(path)` declares `FileNotFoundException` (a subclass of `IOException`) and `BufferedReader.readLine()` declares `IOException`. `javac` requires every checked exception a method body might produce to be caught there or declared in its `throws` clause, and the original `readFirstLine` did neither. The fix declares `throws IOException` on `readFirstLine`, which says truthfully that reading a file can fail for reasons outside the method's control (missing file, disk error). Since `main` calls `readFirstLine` and doesn't catch the exception, `main` needs `throws IOException` too. The obligation keeps moving up the call chain until something catches it or, as here, it leaves `main`, which prints a stack trace and exits with a nonzero status if the file can't be read.

exercises.prompt: What happens when this program runs? Be specific about what prints and what does not.
hints: unitsPerBox declares no throws clause. Does that mean it cannot fail, or only that the compiler isn't tracking whether it can?
Trace the loop through boxCounts = {5, 0, 2} one iteration at a time. What happens on the second iteration?
Once an exception is thrown and nothing catches it, does the loop continue to its next iteration, or does the whole program stop right there?
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints 'Calculating units per box...', then 'Result: 20' for boxCount=5, then throws an uncaught ArithmeticException (/ by zero) on boxCount=0, the program terminates immediately with a stack trace on standard error. 'Result: 50' (for boxCount=2) and 'Done.' never print.
exercises.solutionExplanation: unitsPerBox divides by boxCount, which compiles because ArithmeticException is unchecked (it extends RuntimeException), so the compiler does not require it to be declared or caught. That says nothing about whether it can happen at run time. The first iteration, boxCount = 5, computes 100 / 5 = 20 and prints 'Result: 20'. The second, boxCount = 0, throws ArithmeticException: / by zero as soon as the division runs. Nothing in the call chain catches it, so it propagates out of unitsPerBox and main, the JVM prints a stack trace to standard error, and the process exits with a nonzero status. The third iteration (boxCount = 2) and the final 'Done.' never run, because an uncaught exception ends the whole program, not just the current iteration.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what determines whether an exception class is 'checked' or 'unchecked' in Java?
options: Checked exceptions are checked by the JVM at run time, while unchecked exceptions are only checked by the compiler.
Any exception you create yourself with a custom class is automatically unchecked, while only exceptions from the standard library can be checked.
Checked exceptions represent more severe failures than unchecked exceptions.
An exception is unchecked if it extends RuntimeException (or is an Error); every other subclass of Exception is checked.
assessments.explanation: The checked/unchecked label depends on where a class sits in the Throwable hierarchy: whether it descends from RuntimeException (or is an Error), not on severity. The “Checked exceptions represent more severe failures than unchecked exceptions” option is the classic misconception. Error, which is unchecked, covers some of the most severe failures in the JVM. The “Any exception you create yourself…” option is wrong: a custom exception class is checked or unchecked based purely on which class it extends (Exception vs RuntimeException), regardless of who wrote it. The “Checked exceptions are checked by the JVM…” option has the terminology backwards: checked exceptions are checked by the compiler (at compile time, via javac), while unchecked exceptions get no such enforcement, though both kinds can be thrown and caught at run time.

assessments.prompt: A junior developer asks why Java bothers distinguishing checked from unchecked exceptions at all, and specifically why the compiler doesn't just force every method to declare every exception it could possibly throw, including things like NullPointerException. Explain the reasoning behind the split.
assessments.modelAnswer: The checked/unchecked split exists to apply the compiler's enforcement selectively, to the kinds of failures where that enforcement is useful, rather than universally. Checked exceptions are meant to represent conditions that are external to the code's own logic and that a well-written caller could reasonably anticipate and recover from: a file that doesn't exist, a network call that times out, a database that's briefly unreachable. These are facts about the environment at a particular moment, not defects in the code, and there's value in the compiler forcing every caller along the chain to at least acknowledge that the operation might fail, rather than letting that possibility be ignored. Unchecked exceptions, by contrast, are overwhelmingly subclasses of RuntimeException, and they typically signal a bug in the code: dereferencing something that shouldn't have been null, indexing past an array's bounds, dividing by a value that should have been validated first. If Java required every method to declare throws NullPointerException the moment it dereferenced any object, or throws ArithmeticException the moment it divided two numbers, that requirement would apply to nearly every method in existence, since almost any method can theoretically be called with bad enough input to trigger one of these. The throws clause would balloon into a list of 'basically anything could go wrong here' on every single method signature, which would convey essentially no useful information to a reader and would make the meaningful, specific checked exceptions (the ones worth designing an API around) disappear into that noise. So the split is really a judgment call, baked into the language, about where compiler-enforced acknowledgment earns its cost (specific, external, recoverable conditions) and where it would just add ceremony without adding useful signal (pervasive conditions that are really about incorrect code, not about the environment).

assessments.prompt: A library method is declared as public void loadConfig(String path) throws IOException. A later release changes it to public void loadConfig(String path) throws IOException, SQLException. What is the consequence for existing callers?
options: This change is illegal, and javac refuses to compile the library itself, since a throws clause can never be modified once a method has been published.
Existing already-compiled .class files calling the old version will start throwing SQLException automatically at run time, without needing to recompile at all.
Every existing caller that doesn't already catch or declare SQLException now fails to compile.
None -- adding a new checked exception to a throws clause is always fully backward compatible with existing code.
assessments.explanation: A throws clause is part of a method's public contract, like its parameter types and return type. Callers compiled against the old signature only acknowledged IOException, so after SQLException is added they have an unhandled checked exception, and javac reports a compile error the next time they are rebuilt. The “None -- adding a new checked exception…” option ignores this common source of breaking API changes. The “Existing already-compiled .class files calling the old…” option misunderstands how already-compiled bytecode works: it isn't retroactively altered by a signature change elsewhere. The “This change is illegal, and javac refuses…” option is wrong because changing a throws clause is completely legal from the compiler's point of view; the cost falls on callers, not on the library itself.

assessments.prompt: try { loadConfig("app.config"); } catch (IOException e) { } What is the most accurate critique of this code?
options: It fails to compile, because a catch block handling a checked exception must contain at least one executable statement.
It compiles and technically satisfies javac's requirement, but it silently discards the entire reason the checked exception existed.
It's a fully safe way to satisfy the compiler when a method can't recover from a checked exception -- there's no real downside, since the exception type is at least named in the catch clause.
It's functionally equivalent to declaring throws IOException on the enclosing method, since both approaches satisfy the compiler in the same way.
assessments.explanation: An empty catch block compiles and stops the compiler complaining, but it discards the information the exception carried: the program proceeds as though loadConfig succeeded, with nothing logged and no trace for whoever debugs the broken state later. The “It's a fully safe way to satisfy…” option is the misconception to avoid; naming the exception type in a catch clause that does nothing provides no safety. The “It fails to compile, because a catch…” option is wrong: an empty catch block is completely legal Java, however inadvisable. The “It's functionally equivalent to declaring throws IOException…” option is wrong because declaring throws propagates the exception to a caller who might handle it, while swallowing it here makes it vanish. These have opposite effects on whether the failure is ever visible to anyone.

assessments.prompt: Two methods might each fail: (1) one calls Integer.parseInt(text), which can throw NumberFormatException; (2) one calls new FileInputStream(path), which can throw FileNotFoundException. Which of these, if either, would the compiler actually require to be caught or declared with throws?
options: Only (2), because FileNotFoundException extends IOException, which does not extend RuntimeException and is therefore checked; NumberFormatException extends IllegalArgumentException, which extends RuntimeException, making it unchecked and requiring no such declaration.
Only (1), because NumberFormatException is checked while FileNotFoundException is unchecked.
Neither (1) nor (2), since the compiler only enforces this rule for exceptions raised directly with a throw statement, not ones thrown from inside library methods.
Both (1) and (2), since any exception that can realistically occur in a method's body must be declared or caught.
assessments.explanation: The checked/unchecked distinction depends on where a class sits in the Throwable hierarchy. FileNotFoundException is a subclass of IOException, which is a subclass of Exception that does not extend RuntimeException, so it's checked, and a method whose body might produce it must catch or declare it. NumberFormatException, by contrast, is a subclass of IllegalArgumentException, which extends RuntimeException, so it's unchecked, and the compiler enforces nothing about it regardless of how likely it is to occur. The “Only (1), because NumberFormatException is checked while…” option has the two backwards. The “Both (1) and (2), since any exception…” option is wrong because unchecked exceptions never require this regardless of likelihood. The “Neither (1) nor (2), since the compiler…” option is wrong: the compiler's enforcement applies to any checked exception a method's body might produce, whether via a direct throw or by calling another method (including a library method) that's declared to throw one.

assessments.prompt: While reviewing a pull request you find many methods that catch Exception, log 'error', and return null. Explain the problems this causes and what you would ask the author to do instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: Catching Exception swallows everything, including programming bugs like NullPointerException, so failures are hidden rather than handled. Logging only 'error' without the exception or context loses the stack trace, and returning null pushes the problem to callers who probably do not check it, so the eventual NullPointerException appears far from the cause. Ask the author to catch only the specific exceptions they can handle (for example IOException when a retry or fallback makes sense), and otherwise let exceptions propagate or wrap them in a meaningful domain exception that keeps the cause. Log once at a boundary with the exception object and useful context. Replace null returns with Optional for 'not found' cases or with exceptions for errors, and use try-with-resources so cleanup does not depend on catch blocks.

concepts.title: try, catch, and finally: Handling Exceptions and Building Custom Ones
concepts.description: try/catch matches a thrown exception to the most specific applicable handler in top-to-bottom order, finally runs no matter how the try block ends (including in a surprising interaction with return) and custom exception classes let you give your own failure conditions a name, a message, and a preserved cause.
learningObjectives: Write a try/catch block with multiple catch clauses in the correct order and explain why order matters.
Use multi-catch (catch (A | B e)) to handle multiple unrelated exception types with shared logic.
Explain precisely when a finally block executes relative to return statements and thrown exceptions.
Predict the surprising outcome of a return statement inside both a try block and its finally block.
Define a custom exception class, choosing checked vs unchecked appropriately, with proper constructors and a chained cause.

sections.heading: try and catch: Matching an Exception to the Right Handler
Multi-Catch: One Handler for Several Unrelated Types
finally: Runs No Matter What, Including a Surprising Case with return
Designing Custom Exception Classes

examples.title: Catch Order Matters: The Compiler Rejects an Unreachable catch
examples.explanation: In the broken version, `ArithmeticException` is a subtype of `Exception`, so the first catch clause (`catch (Exception e)`) already matches every `ArithmeticException` that could ever be thrown here, along with anything else that extends `Exception`. That makes the second catch clause permanently unreachable: there's no possible exception that could reach it, since anything it would match was already claimed by the broader clause above. `javac` recognizes this statically and refuses to compile it, rather than letting it become dead code. The fixed version lists the narrower, more specific type first: `ArithmeticException` gets its own targeted handling, and `Exception` remains as a fallback for anything else, which is the general rule for ordering catch clauses: most specific to least specific, top to bottom.

examples.title: finally Runs No Matter What, Even Overriding a return
examples.explanation: The try block prints its message and evaluates return 1, but that return does not complete the method immediately. Java always runs the finally block first, before handing control back to the caller. The finally block prints its own message and then executes return 2, which completes compute() right then and there; the pending return 1 from the try block is discarded, having never taken effect. The program therefore prints both messages, followed by 'result = 2', not 'result = 1'. This is why placing a return (or throw) inside a finally block is considered a serious anti-pattern in code: it can override the intended result of the try block, or swallow an exception that was actively propagating out of it, with zero warning from the compiler.

examples.title: A Custom Checked Exception That Preserves Its Cause
examples.explanation: InsufficientFundsException extends Exception, so it is checked. That is a choice: 'the account doesn't have enough money' is an anticipated, recoverable business condition, not a programming bug. Because withdraw declares throws InsufficientFundsException, javac forces main to catch it or declare it; main catches it and prints the message passed to the constructor, via getMessage(). The second constructor, taking a Throwable cause, is not used in this example. It is there so that a future withdraw that wraps a lower-level failure (say, a database error while checking the balance) can keep the original cause for getCause().

misconceptions.description: Since only one catch block can ever run for a given exception, the order the catch clauses are written in doesn't really matter -- Java will find the right one regardless.
misconceptions.clarification: Order matters critically, because only one catch block runs: Java checks catch clauses strictly top to bottom and executes the body of the FIRST one whose type matches, then stops looking. If a broader supertype is listed before a narrower subtype of it, the narrower catch block becomes permanently unreachable: every exception it could ever match was already claimed by the broader clause above it, and this specific situation is caught by the compiler as an error, not accepted. The safe rule is to always order catch clauses from most specific to least specific.
misconceptions.fact: Order matters critically, because only one catch block runs: Java checks catch clauses strictly top to bottom and executes the body of the FIRST one whose type matches, then stops looking.

misconceptions.description: finally is basically just a place for cleanup code that runs after the try/catch finishes -- equivalent to writing that same code right after the whole try/catch statement.
misconceptions.clarification: finally is not equivalent to code placed after the try/catch block, in two specific, important ways. First, finally runs even when the try or catch block executes a return statement: the return is paused, finally runs, and only then does the method complete (unless finally itself returns or throws, in which case it overrides the pending outcome). Code placed after the try/catch would never run in that case at all, because the method would have already exited via the earlier return. Second, finally runs even when an exception is thrown and not caught by any of the try's catch blocks, it still executes on the way out, before the exception continues propagating to the caller, whereas code placed after the try/catch would never be reached in that scenario, since control never reaches past the point where the uncaught exception escaped.

exercises.prompt: This code fails to compile with: `error: exception NumberFormatException has already been caught`. Explain why, and fix the ordering.
hints: Check the class hierarchy: does NumberFormatException extend RuntimeException, or is it unrelated to it?
The first catch clause here is broader than the second. Would every NumberFormatException that could occur already be caught by the first clause?
Reorder the catch clauses so the more specific type, NumberFormatException, comes before the more general RuntimeException.
exercises.solutionExplanation: NumberFormatException extends IllegalArgumentException, which extends RuntimeException, so it is a subtype of RuntimeException, not an unrelated type. The original code lists catch (RuntimeException e) first, which already matches every NumberFormatException that Integer.parseInt could ever throw, making the second, narrower catch clause permanently unreachable: there's no exception left for it to catch that the first clause wouldn't have already claimed. javac detects this statically and refuses to compile. Swapping the order so NumberFormatException is listed first fixes it: now the more specific, more informative handler runs for number-format failures, and the broader RuntimeException clause remains as a fallback for any other unchecked exception Integer.parseInt might theoretically throw.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print, and what value does it actually return from validate()? Explain the surprising part.
hints: input is -5, so the try block throws IllegalArgumentException before it ever reaches its own return true.
The catch block handles the exception and evaluates return false. But does that return statement complete the method immediately?
finally runs after the catch block's return is evaluated but before the method truly exits, and this finally block has its own return statement. Which one wins?
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints 'checking input: -5', then 'caught: negative input', then 'cleanup running', then 'result: true'. Even though the catch block evaluates return false, the finally block's own return true executes afterward and overrides it: validate() returns true, not false.
exercises.solutionExplanation: With input = -5, the try block prints its message and then throws IllegalArgumentException before reaching return true. The catch clause matches, prints 'caught: negative input', and evaluates return false, but that return is only a pending outcome, not a completed one, because finally must still run before the method can exit. finally prints 'cleanup running' and then executes its own return true, which completes the method right there, discarding the catch block's pending return false. So validate(-5) returns true, and main prints 'result: true': a direct, sharper illustration of the same finally-overrides-return trap: it's not limited to overriding a try block's return, it overrides a catch block's return via the exact same mechanism, which is why a return inside finally is considered dangerous regardless of which earlier block it's overriding.

options: 10, because the try block's return statement executes and completes the method before finally ever runs.
It throws an exception at runtime because two return statements conflict.
This fails to compile, because a method cannot have return statements in both try and finally.
20, because finally always runs before the method actually completes, and its own return statement overrides the try block's pending return.
assessments.explanation: finally always runs after the try block and before the method's completion is finalized, even when that completion would have been a return. Since this finally block has its own return, that return completes the method and the try block's pending return 10 is discarded, so f() returns 20. The “10, because the try block's return statement…” option is the natural but incorrect assumption that a return statement in try immediately and unconditionally exits the method: it doesn't, when a finally block is present. The “This fails to compile, because a method…” option is wrong because this code compiles perfectly fine; having return statements in both try and finally is legal Java, just widely considered poor practice. The “It throws an exception at runtime…” option is wrong because there is no runtime conflict or exception here at all: the behavior is fully deterministic and specified by the language, just frequently surprising to newcomers.

assessments.prompt: Explain the finally-overrides-return trap to a colleague who just discovered it in their own code, and separately explain why a well-designed custom exception class should provide a constructor that accepts a Throwable cause.
assessments.modelAnswer: The finally-overrides-return trap exists because finally is guaranteed to run before a method finishes, however the try or catch block was about to finish, including by a return. When try or catch executes return, that return is a pending outcome, and Java still runs the finally block before finalizing it. If finally itself contains a return (or a throw), that statement completes the method and whatever the try or catch was about to return is discarded, with no compiler warning by default. It is dangerous because it looks reasonable: both blocks return a value, and you can't tell which one wins unless you know this rule. The fix is behavioral, not syntactic: treat finally as a place exclusively for side-effect cleanup (closing resources, releasing locks, logging) and never put a return or throw inside one. On the custom exception question: a constructor that accepts a Throwable cause, typically alongside a String message, lets you wrap a lower-level exception in a more meaningful, higher-level one without losing the original failure's identity and stack trace. If a method catches a low-level exception like SQLException and wants to re-throw something more meaningful to its own callers, like OrderProcessingException, throwing it WITHOUT passing the original exception as a cause means that anyone who later prints the stack trace or calls getCause() on the new exception sees nothing about the SQLException that triggered the problem: the debugging information you'd want most when something fails in production. Providing that (message, cause) constructor, and consistently using it whenever you're wrapping an underlying failure, costs almost nothing and preserves an important diagnostic trail.

assessments.prompt: Which of these two multi-catch declarations fails to compile, and why? (A) catch (SQLException | IOException e) { ... } (B) catch (FileNotFoundException | IOException e) { ... }
options: Neither fails to compile; both are completely valid multi-catch declarations as written.
Both (A) and (B) fail to compile, since multi-catch can only ever combine two unrelated subtypes of RuntimeException specifically.

(B) fails to compile, because FileNotFoundException is itself a subtype of IOException -- the second alternative in the pair can never add anything the first doesn't already cover, and Java specifically disallows multi-catching a type alongside one of its own subtypes.
(A) fails to compile, because SQLException and IOException share no common supertype other than Exception itself.
assessments.explanation: Multi-catch requires that neither listed type be a subtype of the other, since that makes one alternative redundant. (B) violates this: FileNotFoundException extends IOException, so everything the first alternative matches is already covered by the second. (A) is legal: SQLException and IOException are unrelated, which is the situation multi-catch exists for. The “(A) fails to compile, because SQLException…” option is wrong about which pair is the problem. The “Both (A) and (B) fail to compile…” option invents a restriction to RuntimeException subtypes that doesn't exist: multi-catch works with checked exception types too, as (A) demonstrates. The “Neither fails to compile; both are completely…” option is wrong because (B) is a compile error.

assessments.prompt: try { Object[] items = new String[3]; items[0] = 42; } catch (ArrayStoreException e) { System.out.println("store error"); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("runtime error"); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println("general error"); } Given that ArrayStoreException extends RuntimeException, what happens when this is compiled and run?
options: It compiles fine but prints "runtime error" instead, because RuntimeException is always checked before any of its subtypes at run time, regardless of catch order they happen to be written in.
It compiles fine and prints "store error", because ArrayStoreException is listed first and is the most specific type matching the exception actually thrown by storing an int into a String array.
It throws an uncaught exception at run time, since none of the three catch clauses can actually match a store error.
It fails to compile, because listing ArrayStoreException before RuntimeException before Exception, in that order, makes the later clauses unreachable.
assessments.explanation: items is declared as Object[] but refers to a String[] at run time; assigning items[0] = 42 (autoboxed to Integer) attempts to store an Integer into an array whose element type is String, which throws ArrayStoreException. The catch clauses here are ordered correctly: most specific (ArrayStoreException) first, then its broader supertype RuntimeException, then the broadest, Exception, so this compiles fine, and since ArrayStoreException is thrown, the first, most specific matching clause runs, printing "store error". The “It fails to compile, because listing ArrayStoreException…” option misapplies the unreachable-catch rule, which only flags a narrower clause placed AFTER a broader one already covering it: the order here is the reverse, and correct. The “It compiles fine but prints "runtime error"…” option invents a run-time matching mechanism Java doesn't have; catch matching always respects the written top-to-bottom order. The “It throws an uncaught exception at run…” option is wrong because the first clause matches.

assessments.prompt: A class is designed to signal that a withdrawal amount exceeds an account's balance -- a normal, anticipated business condition callers should be able to handle. Which custom exception design is most appropriate?
options: class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception { ... }, with constructors accepting a message and, separately, a message plus a Throwable cause.
class InsufficientFundsException extends Error { ... } -- since running out of funds is a serious problem for the account holder.
class InsufficientFundsException extends RuntimeException { ... } -- since callers should never be forced by the compiler to acknowledge an ordinary business condition.
class InsufficientFundsException extends Throwable { ... } directly, bypassing both Exception and Error entirely for maximum design flexibility.
assessments.explanation: Insufficient funds is the kind of anticipated, recoverable condition checked exceptions are meant for. It is not a bug, and a caller (a UI showing an error, a batch job logging and skipping the transaction) can be expected to handle it. Extending Exception makes it checked, and providing both a message-only and a message-plus-cause constructor is the standard, low-cost convention that supports clear error messages now and cause-chaining if a future implementation needs to wrap a lower-level failure. The “class InsufficientFundsException extends RuntimeException { ... }…” option would let callers ignore a condition the design intends them to consider. The “class InsufficientFundsException extends Error { ... }…” option is wrong: Error is reserved for serious JVM-level problems the application isn't expected to recover from, not ordinary business rule violations. The “class InsufficientFundsException extends Throwable { ... }…” option needlessly discards the well-understood Exception/Error distinction the rest of the language and ecosystem rely on.

concepts.title: try-with-resources and AutoCloseable
concepts.description: try-with-resources closes every AutoCloseable resource at the end of a block, in reverse order of declaration, even when an exception is thrown. That removes two failure modes of manual finally-based cleanup: the easy-to-get-wrong null check around close(), and a close() failure that destroys information about the exception already propagating.
learningObjectives: Explain the resource-leak and lost-exception problems try-with-resources was introduced to solve, compared to manual close() in a finally block.
Write a try-with-resources statement with one or more resources and explain the exact order they are closed in.
Implement a custom class that implements AutoCloseable so it can be used directly in a try-with-resources statement.
Explain what a suppressed exception is, when one occurs, and how to retrieve it.
Explain why a resource used in try-with-resources must be effectively final.

examples.title: Before and After: Manual finally Cleanup vs try-with-resources
examples.explanation: The 'before' version needs reader declared and initialized to null outside the try so finally can still reference it even if the FileReader constructor itself throws before reader is ever assigned a value, and the null check exists purely to avoid a NullPointerException in that specific failure path. If readLine() throws and close() also throws while cleaning up, the close() exception overwrites the readLine() exception, hiding the root cause. The 'after' version eliminates both concerns: the resource is declared in the try's parentheses, closed automatically no matter how the block exits, and if both the body and the automatic close both throw, the body's exception is preserved as primary with close()'s exception attached as suppressed rather than lost.

examples.title: Multiple Resources Close in Reverse Order
examples.explanation: The three resources are opened in the order they're declared: A, then B, then C, which prints 'open A', 'open B', 'open C' before the try block's body even runs. Once the body finishes ('using A, B, C'), Java closes the resources automatically in the EXACT REVERSE of that declaration order: C first, then B, then A, printing 'close C', 'close B', 'close A'. This mirrors how these resources would typically depend on each other in code (a later-declared resource, like a database Statement, is often built from and depends on an earlier one, like a Connection, so tearing down the more-dependent one first, before the resource it depends on, is the safer order).

examples.title: Suppressed Exceptions When close() Also Fails
examples.explanation: doWork() throws while the body is still executing, and that RuntimeException becomes the primary exception. Before it propagates out of the try statement, Java runs close() on the resource, and close() also throws, this time an IllegalStateException. Instead of letting it replace the exception already in flight (the old finally-block problem), try-with-resources attaches it to the primary exception as a suppressed exception. The catch block prints 'caught: work failed', showing the original failure is the one caught, then iterates getSuppressed() and prints 'suppressed: close failed too'. Neither failure is lost, and it is clear which one came first.

misconceptions.description: If an exception occurs while automatically closing a resource in try-with-resources, it silently overwrites or replaces whatever exception the try block's body itself had already thrown.
misconceptions.clarification: The opposite is true, and this is the problem try-with-resources was designed to fix. If the try body throws AND the automatic close() also throws, the body's exception stays the PRIMARY exception that propagates, and the exception from close() is attached to it as a suppressed exception, retrievable via getSuppressed(). (If only close() throws, with the body completing normally, that close() exception propagates, since there is no earlier exception to suppress it under.)

misconceptions.description: Any object can be used in a try-with-resources statement as long as it happens to have a method literally named close().
misconceptions.clarification: The compiler requires the resource's declared type to implement java.lang.AutoCloseable (or its subinterface Closeable). A method that happens to be spelled close(), without implementing the interface, is not enough and produces a compile-time error such as 'incompatible types: ClassName cannot be converted to AutoCloseable'. The requirement is the interface, not a method name the compiler looks for.

exercises.prompt: This code is meant to safely read and print a file's first line, closing the reader no matter what happens. Instead, it can throw a NullPointerException from inside the finally block itself when the file doesn't exist. Find the bug and fix it using try-with-resources.
hints: If `new FileReader(path)` throws because the file doesn't exist, is `reader` ever assigned before control jumps to finally?
finally still runs even when the initialization line in the try block throws. What does reader.close() do if reader is still null at that point?
Rewrite this using try-with-resources, declaring the BufferedReader in the try's parentheses, and remove the manual finally block.
exercises.solutionExplanation: In the original code, if `new FileReader(path)` throws (for example, FileNotFoundException because the path doesn't exist), that exception happens while reader still holds its initial value of null: the assignment to reader never completes. Control then jumps to finally, which unconditionally calls reader.close(), and since reader is still null at that point, this throws NullPointerException, masking the original, more meaningful FileNotFoundException. The try-with-resources version sidesteps this class of bug completely: the resource is declared and initialized in the try's own parentheses, and Java only attempts to close a resource that was successfully initialized in the first place: if the FileReader construction itself fails, there's no resource to close at all, and the original exception propagates cleanly with nothing extra masking it.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print, and in what order? Pay close attention to the order resources are opened versus closed.
hints: Resources are opened in the order they are declared in the parentheses: outer first, then inner.
The try block's body runs fully before either resource is closed at all.
Resources are closed in the reverse of the order they were opened. Which one is closed first?
exercises.expectedAnswer:
[open] outer
[open] inner
[outer] starting work
[inner] doing detail work
[close] inner
[close] outer
done
exercises.solutionExplanation: The two resources are constructed in declaration order, so 'outer' opens before 'inner': '[open] outer' then '[open] inner'. The try block's body then runs completely, printing both log lines: '[outer] starting work' and '[inner] doing detail work'. Once the body finishes, Java automatically closes the resources in the exact REVERSE of their declaration order: inner (opened second) is closed first, then outer (opened first) is closed last: '[close] inner' then '[close] outer'. Finally, 'done' prints after the entire try-with-resources statement, including all of its automatic closing, has completed.

assessments.prompt: Inside a try-with-resources block, the body throws a RuntimeException, and the automatic close() call on the resource also throws an exception while cleaning up. What actually happens?
options: The program deadlocks, because two exceptions cannot be resolved during the same try-with-resources statement.
Both exceptions are silently discarded, and the try-with-resources statement simply completes as if nothing had gone wrong.
The original RuntimeException from the body propagates as the primary exception, with the exception from close() attached to it as a suppressed exception, retrievable via getSuppressed().
The exception from close() replaces the original RuntimeException entirely, and only the close() exception is ever visible to the caller.
assessments.explanation: try-with-resources treats the body's exception as primary and propagates it, attaching any exception from the automatic close() as a suppressed exception instead of losing it. That is the improvement over manual finally-based cleanup, where a failing close() inside finally could replace the exception already propagating. The “The exception from close() replaces the original…” option describes that older failure mode, which try-with-resources fixes. The “Both exceptions are silently discarded…” option is wrong: neither exception is discarded; the primary one propagates and the second is preserved as suppressed information on it. The “The program deadlocks, because two exceptions cannot…” option is fabricated: there's no deadlock mechanism involved in exception handling here at all.

assessments.prompt: Explain to someone still manually closing resources in finally blocks why try-with-resources is considered strictly safer, referencing both the closing order for multiple resources and the concept of a suppressed exception.
assessments.modelAnswer: Manual cleanup in a finally block has two recurring problems. You need a null check before calling close(), because the resource's construction might have failed before it was assigned. And if close() throws while an exception from the try block is already propagating, the close() exception overwrites the original, so whoever handles it sees only the often less informative cleanup failure, with no trace of the root cause. try-with-resources addresses both. First, the resource is declared and initialized inside the try statement's parentheses, and Java closes only a resource that was successfully constructed, so there is no half-initialized resource for a finally block to mishandle with a null check. Second, when the try body throws AND the automatic close() also throws, Java doesn't let the close() exception replace the original, it keeps the body's exception as the primary one that propagates to the caller, and attaches the close() exception to it as a suppressed exception, retrievable through getSuppressed(). Nothing is lost: a careful caller can inspect both the primary failure and whatever went wrong during cleanup. On ordering, when a try-with-resources statement declares several resources they are closed in the reverse of the order they were opened. The most recently opened, usually most dependent, resource is torn down first (a Statement built from a Connection is closed before that Connection). All of this happens automatically, without the programmer hand-writing and re-verifying the null checks, ordering, and exception preservation that manual finally cleanup requires.

assessments.prompt: class Widget { public void close() { System.out.println("closing"); } } -- Widget does NOT implement AutoCloseable. try (Widget w = new Widget()) { } What happens when this is compiled?
options: It fails to compile, because the compiler requires the resource's declared type to actually implement java.lang.AutoCloseable (or Closeable) -- merely having a same-named close() method, without formally implementing that interface, does not satisfy the requirement.
It fails to compile, but only because Widget's close() method fails to declare throws Exception.
It compiles fine but never actually calls close() at run time, since Widget isn't a recognized built-in resource type.
It compiles fine, because Widget has a method literally named close(), and that alone is all try-with-resources actually requires.
assessments.explanation: try-with-resources is interface-based: the compiler checks that the resource's declared type implements AutoCloseable (or its subinterface Closeable), not merely that it has a method spelled close(). Widget has the right method name but no implements clause, so the compiler rejects it with an incompatible-types error. The “It compiles fine, because Widget has…” option describes a naming-convention check the compiler does not perform. The “It compiles fine but never actually calls…” option is wrong because this code doesn't compile at all, so nothing about it ever reaches run time. The “It fails to compile, but only…” option is wrong: AutoCloseable's close() is declared to throw Exception, but an implementing class is always free to narrow that to no declared exception at all, which is what Widget's close() does; that's not the problem here.

assessments.prompt: class CleanResource implements AutoCloseable { void doWork() { System.out.println("working"); } public void close() { throw new IllegalStateException("close failed"); } } try (CleanResource r = new CleanResource()) { r.doWork(); } What happens?
options: The exception from close() is automatically suppressed and discarded, since suppression applies to any exception thrown by an automatic close() call.
IllegalStateException("close failed") propagates out of the try statement as an ordinary, unsuppressed exception.
The try statement completes with no visible effect at all, since the body itself never threw anything.
This throws a NullPointerException, because a resource cannot be closed unless something in the try body already failed first.
assessments.explanation: doWork() runs and completes normally, printing "working", so no exception is in flight from the body. When close() is then called automatically and throws IllegalStateException, there is no primary exception to suppress it under, so it becomes the exception that propagates out of the try statement, as if thrown. The “The try statement completes with no visible…” option ignores that close()'s own exception still has to go somewhere. The “The exception from close() is automatically suppressed…” option misapplies suppression: suppression only happens when BOTH the body and close() throw; a lone close() failure is never suppressed, since suppression is additive information attached to a primary exception that doesn't exist here. The “This throws a NullPointerException, because a resource…” option invents a precondition on closing that Java's try-with-resources doesn't have: close() always runs at the end of the block, body failure or not.
